startingBoard.title: The Chessboard and Piece Setup
startingBoard.subtitle: The chessboard has 64 squares: 32 light and 32 dark. Squares are identified by vertical files (a-h) and horizontal ranks (1-8).
startingBoard.clickHint: Click on any square to discover its coordinate and piece.
startingBoard.rule1Text: When setting up the board, each player must have a light square in their bottom-right corner (h1 and a8).
startingBoard.rule2Text: The White Queen always starts on a light square (d1), and the Black Queen on a dark square (d8). The King stands next to her on the e-file.
startingBoard.rule3Text: All 8 white pawns stand on the 2nd rank and all 8 black pawns on the 7th rank, shielding the pieces behind them.

pieces.title: Chess Pieces and Movement Rules
pieces.subtitle: Every piece has a unique role and moving style. Pick a piece to see its movement lines on the demonstration board.
pieces.note: Note: Pieces cannot land on squares occupied by friendly pieces. An opponent piece is captured by landing on its square.

king.name: King
king.summary: Moves only 1 square in any direction.
king.description: The King is the most precious piece. If the King cannot escape attack (checkmate), the game ends. The King steps one square in any direction, but can never walk into danger.

queen.name: Queen
queen.summary: Moves any number of open squares vertically, horizontally, or diagonally.
queen.description: The Queen is the most powerful piece. It combines the powers of the Rook and Bishop, sliding across ranks, files, and diagonals as far as the way is clear.

rook.name: Rook
rook.summary: Moves in straight lines (vertically and horizontally).
rook.description: The Rook is a mighty long-range piece. It travels along vertical and horizontal lines across any number of empty squares, but cannot jump over other pieces.

bishop.name: Bishop
bishop.description: Each player has two Bishops: one on light squares and one on dark squares. A Bishop never changes its square color and glides freely across open diagonals.

knight.name: Knight
knight.summary: Jumping piece: moves in an 'L' shape and leaps over obstacles.
knight.description: The Knight is the only piece that can jump over others. It hops two squares in one direction and one square sideways, changing square color on every single leap.

pawn.name: Pawn
pawn.summary: Brave pawn: moves straight forward, captures diagonally.
pawn.description: Pawns march forward and can never move backward. On their very first move, they may advance two squares. They capture one square diagonally. Reaching the far end allows promotion to a Queen or another piece.

goals.title: Goal of the Game: Check, Checkmate and Stalemate
goals.subtitle: The main goal in chess is not to capture every single piece, but to deliver checkmate to the enemy King.

shah.title: Check (Attack)
shah.simpleExplain: Check occurs when the King is under direct attack.
shah.detail: When an opponent piece threatens to capture your King, it is check. You must save the King immediately: run to a safe square, block the attack with another piece, or capture the attacking piece.
shah.note: Check rule: When the King is attacked, it must be protected right away. The King is never captured or removed from the board.

mat.title: Checkmate (Victory)
mat.simpleExplain: The King is under attack and has no way to escape.
mat.detail: Checkmate is the ultimate goal in chess. If the King is in check and cannot move away, block the attack, or capture the attacker, the game ends instantly and the attacker wins.
mat.note: Checkmate rule: The King is attacked and has no legal escape. The player delivering checkmate wins the game.

pat.title: Stalemate (Draw)
pat.simpleExplain: The King is not attacked, but there are no legal moves.
pat.detail: If the player whose turn it is has no legal move and their King is NOT in check, the game is in stalemate. Stalemate immediately results in a peaceful draw.
pat.note: Stalemate condition: The player to move has no legal moves and their King is safe. The game ends in a tie.

draw.title: Other Draws
draw.detail: When neither player has enough pieces left to force checkmate (such as King vs King or King and Bishop vs King), the game ends in an automatic draw. Threefold repetition of the same position also leads to a draw.
draw.note: Draw rule: When checkmate cannot be forced or both players mutually agree, the game is declared a draw.

specialMoves.title: Special Chess Moves
specialMoves.subtitle: Learn the rules of castling, pawn promotion, and en passant.

castling.title: Castling
castling.subtitle: Defense and Attack Combined
castling.description: The only double move in chess, designed to shield your King and activate your corner Rook.
castling.stepDesc: Kingside castling: The King slides two squares from e1 to g1, and the h1 Rook hops over to f1.
rules: The King and the castling Rook must not have moved yet.
All squares between the King and the Rook must be empty.
The King must not be in check and cannot pass through attacked squares.

promotion.title: Pawn Promotion
promotion.subtitle: Reaching the Summit
promotion.description: When a pawn reaches the farthest rank of the board, it transforms into a more powerful piece.
promotion.stepDesc: Upon reaching the 8th rank, the pawn immediately turns into a Queen or any chosen piece.
rules: Promotion takes place on the exact turn the pawn lands on the last rank.
The Queen is chosen most often, though tactical Knight underpromotions also occur.
You can have multiple Queens on the board at the same time.

enpassant.title: En Passant
enpassant.subtitle: Special Pawn Strike
enpassant.description: Applies when an enemy pawn jumps two squares forward on its first move and lands right beside yours.
enpassant.stepDesc: When black moves from d7 to d5, the white pawn captures by stepping diagonally onto d6.
rules: Only valid when the opponent pawn advances two squares on a single turn.
The capture must be made on the very next move, or the right is permanently lost.
The captured pawn is removed from the board, and your pawn takes the square it skipped over.

tips.title: 6 Golden Rules for Beginners
tips.subtitle: Remember these simple principles to develop strong chess habits in your opening games.

items.title: Control the Center
items.text: The four central squares (e4, d4, e5, d5) are the keys to controlling the game. Aim your opening pawns toward the center.

items.title: Develop Your Pieces Quickly
items.text: Bring your knights and bishops into the game early. Avoid moving the same piece multiple times without a clear reason.

items.title: Keep Your King Safe
items.text: Castle early to tuck your King away from danger in the center and connect your rooks to open files.

items.title: Do Not Bring the Queen Out Too Soon
items.text: The Queen is very powerful. Bringing it out too early lets minor opponent pieces chase it while developing freely.

items.title: Think Before Every Move
items.text: Always ask yourself: "What is the goal of my opponent's last move? What piece are they threatening?"

items.title: Learn from Every Defeat
items.text: Every lost game is a valuable lesson. Review your moves to discover where you lost focus and improve.

faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions
faq.subtitle: Quick answers to the questions parents and young beginners ask most.

items.question: At what age can children start learning chess?
items.answer: Ages 5-6 are usually ideal to start chess. Children can easily grasp piece movements and simple rules at this age.

items.question: Is any prior experience required to begin?
items.answer: No previous experience is needed. Lessons start from board squares and piece names, explained in simple terms.

items.question: How does chess support a child's development?
items.answer: Chess fosters logical thinking, concentration, patience, spatial awareness, and decisive problem-solving.

items.question: How do we register for lessons?
items.answer: You can sign up by clicking the "Join" button in the navbar or leaving your phone number in the contact form.

items.question: Is it necessary to play against opponents right away?
items.answer: Not at all. In the beginning, learning the rules, piece movements, and solving fun puzzles is much more important.

history.title: Chess Heritage of Azerbaijan
history.lead: Azerbaijan has a deep chess heritage and an internationally celebrated chess academy.
paragraphs: In the East, chess has been revered for centuries as the royal game of intellect; the celebrated poet Nizami Ganjavi wove chess terminology into his timeless verse.
In modern times, Azerbaijani teams have claimed European Championships, nurturing numerous world-renowned grandmasters.
Enthusiasm among children continues to grow, and our academy is dedicated to providing young learners with an inspiring foundation.
